stories.headline: Trump-Endorsed Candidates Face Key Tests in Georgia and Alabama Senate Primary Runoffs
stories.summary:
Voters in Georgia, Alabama, Oklahoma, and Washington, D.C. headed to the polls Tuesday in a series of primary runoffs and elections that will determine party nominees for high-stakes Senate and gubernatorial contests. The results offer a fresh measure of President Trump's endorsement power heading into the 2026 midterm cycle.

In Georgia, Trump made a last-minute endorsement of Rep. Mike Collins in the Republican primary runoff to challenge Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country. Alabama also features a contested Republican Senate runoff. Both states are considered critical battlegrounds for control of the Senate in November.

The primaries are seen as an early indicator of whether Trump's endorsement remains a decisive force in Republican primaries, following a mixed track record in recent electoral cycles. Results from the evening's contests were expected to set the table for the general election campaigns in earnest.

Washington, D.C. voters were simultaneously choosing party nominees for mayor and congressional delegate, adding a separate local dynamic to a busy primary night across four jurisdictions.

stories.headline: Hungary's Parliament Amends Constitution to Bar Orbán from Returning as Prime Minister
stories.summary:
Hungary's parliament voted Tuesday to amend the country's constitution, capping a prime minister's tenure at eight years and effectively barring former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán from ever returning to the role. The measure passed 135 to 50, pushed through by the Tisza party's two-thirds supermajority under new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who swept Orbán from power in April's election.

The amendment applies retroactively to all prime ministers since 1990, meaning Orbán — who governed Hungary uninterrupted for 16 years — is permanently disqualified from the office. Magyar himself would also be limited to serving until 2034 under the same provision. The law requires only the signature of President Tamás Sulyok to take effect.

Orbán and his depleted Fidesz party voted against the measure and condemned it as political persecution. Orbán's former political director, Balázs Orbán, accused Magyar of 'using political power to exclude a political opponent from democratic competition.' Orbán himself wrote on Facebook: 'If I'm needed, I'll be here.'

The constitutional change is part of a broader effort by the Magyar government to dismantle institutions built during the Fidesz era, including the dissolution of Orbán's Sovereignty Protection Office and steps to reclaim state assets transferred to politically connected public trust foundations. The European Commission recently agreed to unlock €16.4 billion in previously withheld EU funds, contingent on anti-corruption reforms now moving through parliament.

stories.headline: Russian Putin Critic Shot Dead in Poland Near Belarusian Consulate; Two Belarusian Nationals Detained
stories.summary:
Polish police are investigating the execution-style killing of Russian artist and Kremlin critic Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot five times in a car park in the city of Białą Podlaską on Monday. The location — roughly 40 kilometers from the Belarusian border and approximately 600 meters from the Belarusian consulate — has drawn immediate attention from investigators.

Kuzovkov, 44, was known for caricatures mocking Vladimir Putin, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko, and Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov. Video posted on social media showed him attending a Russia Day protest outside the Russian embassy in Berlin just days before his death, where he carried a painting caricaturing Putin and Stalin.

Polish prosecutors said an unidentified gunman shot the victim twice, then approached the fallen man and fired three more shots before fleeing. Two Belarusian citizens aged 33 and 37 were detained near the consulate, though their precise roles had not been established as of Tuesday. An autopsy is scheduled for Wednesday.

The killing raises immediate concerns about a state-directed assassination on European Union soil, echoing previous cases of Kremlin critics killed abroad. Polish authorities have not publicly attributed responsibility, and the investigation is ongoing.

stories.headline: SpaceX Acquires AI Startup Cursor for $60 Billion Days After Record-Breaking IPO
stories.summary:
SpaceX has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence startup Cursor in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $60 billion, the company announced Tuesday. The deal comes just days after SpaceX completed what is being described as the largest initial public offering in history, raising $75 billion to fund the company's expansion ambitions.

The acquisition is intended to bolster Elon Musk's artificial intelligence ambitions, folding Cursor's AI capabilities into SpaceX's growing technology portfolio. Cursor is a prominent AI-assisted coding platform that has gained significant traction among software developers.

The timing — capitalizing on newly available public capital within days of the IPO — signals an aggressive expansion strategy. The $60 billion price tag for a single AI startup underscores the extraordinary valuations being attached to advanced AI tooling companies amid fierce competition between major technology players.

The deal adds to a consolidating AI landscape in which large technology and aerospace firms are racing to acquire foundational AI capabilities. SpaceX's move into AI software via a major acquisition represents a significant strategic pivot beyond its core launch and satellite businesses.

stories.headline: Update: Israeli Strike on Beirut Threatens U.S.-Iran Peace Deal as Signing Ceremony Approaches
stories.summary:
The U.S.-Iran peace deal, brokered by Pakistan and set for a signing ceremony Friday in Switzerland, faces a serious test after Israel struck Hezbollah targets in Beirut, drawing warnings from Tehran that the attack could derail the agreement. The deal, described by Vice President Vance as "about a page and a half" and "very general," would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict that began with the U.S.-Israeli strike on Iran on February 28, but leaves Iran's nuclear program issues deferred for later negotiations.

Iran has seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz in the days since the deal was announced, and Iranian officials have stated that Tehran will continue to assert the right to control passage through the waterway. The framework's vagueness on core issues has prompted skepticism from analysts, who warn that the gap between the two sides on nuclear matters remains wide and that the Lebanon dimension adds further instability.

Energy markets, which saw sharp swings following the February outbreak of hostilities, rose on news of the agreement but remain volatile. Experts caution that the war's economic impact on global supply chains will persist for months regardless of whether the deal holds.

The Israeli strike is the most significant new development since the deal was announced, as it introduces a third-party variable that neither Washington nor Tehran fully controls. Trump has urged Israeli restraint, but has not publicly condemned the Beirut attack, leaving the deal's survival uncertain ahead of Friday's scheduled signing.

stories.headline: Wyoming Becomes First U.S. State to Issue Its Own Stablecoin Cryptocurrency
stories.summary:
Wyoming has launched the first state-issued stablecoin in the United States, pegged at $1 and backed by state reserves, marking a significant experiment in government-issued digital currency at the sub-federal level. The move positions Wyoming — already a recognized hub for crypto-friendly regulation — as a potential model for other states considering their own digital currency programs.

Proponents argue that a state-backed stablecoin could streamline government payments, reduce transaction costs, and attract further financial technology investment to the state. Critics and financial regulators have raised questions about systemic risk, the adequacy of reserve backing, and how state-issued digital currencies would interact with federal monetary authority and any eventual federal stablecoin framework.

The development comes as Congress continues to debate national stablecoin legislation, and Wyoming's experiment could either accelerate that process by demonstrating viability or complicate it by introducing a fragmented state-by-state approach. Federal Reserve officials and Treasury Department watchers have been monitoring state-level cryptocurrency initiatives closely as the U.S. works to define its regulatory posture on digital assets.

The Wyoming stablecoin is being closely watched by other states weighing similar moves, as well as by international observers tracking the United States' evolving approach to government-backed digital currency.

stories.headline: Global Trust in News Falls to Record Low, Reuters Institute Survey Finds
stories.summary:
Public trust in news media has reached its lowest point since the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism began tracking it in 2015, with global trust falling three percentage points to 37 percent, according to a major annual survey of nearly 100,000 people across 48 markets published Tuesday. In the United States, trust stands at 25 percent overall and drops to just 15 percent among right-leaning Americans. The UK recorded a five-point decline to 30 percent — 20 points lower than a decade ago.

The report found that more than half of respondents now access news primarily through social media and video platforms, though confidence in those formats is even lower than in traditional news, at 22 percent. Trust in AI chatbots for news information stands at 20 percent globally, though weekly use of AI for news has grown from 7 to 10 percent overall and to 16 percent among adults under 35.

Among individual outlets, CBS News and Fox News each saw trust fall by 10 percentage points from 2025, while CNN dropped six points — suggesting the erosion is not confined to any single part of the political spectrum. The institute attributed the decline to audience anxiety, disengagement, and dissatisfaction with how outlets cover persistent issues including immigration, inflation, and international conflict.

Despite the erosion of trust, the report noted that support for impartial journalism remains high and largely stable, and that audiences appear open to new formats — suggesting the problem may be with execution rather than the concept of news itself.
